Brown dwarf stars are defined by their apparent size, relative mass, radiation and temperature. It's still debated whether or not fusion had to have occurred in its past to for it to qualify.

By EU theory the internal fusion in a star being the force to power it has been easily contested. Primarily because of the convection problem, but also for temperature differences between lower and upper atmospheres, acceleration of particles from CMAs, and the neutrino discrepency. With fusion irrelevant to a star's characteristics, this leaves only it's temperature, luminosity, and radiation levels to distinguish it from a planet. It also removes the mass limitations as a critical mass necessary for pressure induced fusion is no longer relevant.

With mass and fusion requirements removed, Venus meets all other requirements for brown dwarf star classification. It has a temperature (600-750K) within the range of a T class brown dwarf classification (not the lowest acceptable by the way); it emits it's own microwave and infrared radiation, detectable on the night side; and it has been found to be highly electrically active. This is an image of the electrically scarred surface of Venus. And this is an image of plasma activity patterns across the Sun. This comparison suggests to me that similar, although radically different amounts, of electric activity are occurring on the surface of both, Venus and our Sun.

Without the mass driven fusion model, does this qualify our second planet as a brown dwarf star? If an observer in a distant solar system was viewing ours would they see the radiation from Venus as evidence for a binary star system the way we see their sun and companion brown dwarf, like Gliese 229B?
Could Venus be considered a brown dwarf star?

Can someone explain what is happening to whatever he's frying here. How do you turn food (potatoes it looks like) into jumping beans?

Ok, I'm sorry but I have the cooking knowledge of a baby. I burn ramen. What does the pressure was to much mean, and for that matter what does bubbled mean in this context?

When he was deep frying the lard the water on the inside of the little ball evaporated into a gas, then the pressure of the gas building up popped open the ball and that's what made it jump. So its sort of like if you have ever made instant mashed potatoes. You get the water boiling then you add the little powder that absorbs the water and expands. But the water is still evaporating and has not cooled down yet so the extremely hot mashed potatoes boils and pops and sprays you with really hot shit.
He was deep frying potato gnocchi and gasses inside the potato pop out if it's cooked too long.
